source.author: ov
source.text: Qui cum nec prodere visum dedecus auderet, cupiens efferre sub auras, nec posset reticere tamen, secedit humumque effodit et, domini quales aspexerit aures, voce refert parva terraeque immurmurat haustae, indiciumque suae vocis tellure regesta obruit et scrobibus tacitus discedit opertis.
source.text_original: Qui cum nec prodere visum / dedecus auderet, cupiens efferre sub auras, / nec posset reticere tamen, secedit humumque / effodit et, domini quales aspexerit aures, / voce refert parva terraeque immurmurat haustae, / indiciumque suae vocis tellure regesta / obruit et scrobibus tacitus discedit opertis.
source.text_english: When he did not dare to betray the disgrace he had seen, yet, wishing to carry it into the open air and being unable to keep silent, he withdrew, dug up the ground, and, with a tiny voice, told the earth what sort of ears of his master he had seen. Then he murmured it into the earth he had scooped out, and, once the earth had been thrown back over it, he buried the evidence of his own voice and went away in silence, covering the pits.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: in scrobibus cruor et largus Phlegethontis aperti stagnat honos, saevoque vocat grandaeva tumultu Thessalis exanimes atavos magnaeque nepotem Pleiones.
reuse.text_original: in scrobibus cruor et largus Phlegethontis aperti / stagnat honos, saevoque vocat grandaeva tumultu / Thessalis exanimes atavos magnaeque nepotem / Pleiones.
reuse.text_english: in the pits, blood and the abundant glory of open Phlegethon lie stagnant, and in savage uproar aged Thessaly calls the lifeless ancestors and the descendant of great Pleione.
